speaker: John Ketchum
title: NextEra Energy CEO: Powering AI and Nuclear's Comeback
question: In US power markets, why do AI hyperscalers contract directly for dedicated new generation rather than just buying electricity off the grid?
guest: First of all, they are looking to buy electricity off the grid, but a lot of that excess supply of electricity is gone. Second, the hyperscalers are very sensitive about taking electrons off the grid that could drive up prices for retail customers. They've all signed the ratepayer protection pledge, where they've said, "We're going to bring our own generation and match that generation with our data center." If they say, "I'm going to build a data center in state X," they want to make sure they have generation that can power it so they aren't taking away capacity or energy that could otherwise serve another customer and chase up their power prices. They want to bring their own generation to make sure they're paying their own way. And government policy is shifting too, no matter what state you're in. Look at what FERC is doing as they analyze PJM, MISO, SPP, and all the different models around the country—they're all predicated on the same thing: if you're going to build a data center, you have to make sure you pay for the power that goes along with it.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Hyperscalers contract for dedicated generation mainly because the grid cannot deliver the power they need, at the scale and speed they need it.

The binding constraint is time-to-power. A single AI campus can require hundreds of megawatts to several gigawatts, and utilities in many regions quote multi-year waits for interconnection and transmission upgrades. Bringing or underwriting their own generation, sometimes co-located or behind the meter, can cut years off that timeline.

Supply adequacy is the second reason. Markets like PJM and ERCOT face tightening reserve margins, and capacity prices have spiked. Regulators and utilities increasingly require large loads to bring new supply or pay for it, so that existing ratepayers do not bear the costs. Contracting for new capacity eases both the physical and the political obstacles.

Third is price certainty. Long-term power purchase agreements, typically 10 to 20 years, hedge against volatile wholesale and capacity prices. Those contracts also give developers the revenue certainty needed to finance new plants.

Finally, the companies have carbon-free energy commitments. Grid power is a mixed fuel blend, whereas dedicated nuclear, solar, storage or geothermal contracts let them claim clean, additional supply.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
AI hyperscalers contract directly for dedicated new generation primarily because existing US grids cannot deliver massive, round-the-clock power fast enough. Securing standard grid service for a gigawatt-scale data center often means waiting five to ten years for interconnection studies and transmission upgrades—an untenable delay in the AI race. Funding dedicated, often co-located plants lets companies bypass congested transmission bottlenecks or qualify for fast-track "bring your own new generation" pathways established by grid operators like PJM and ERCOT.

Beyond speed, regional grids lack the spare firm capacity to absorb huge constant loads without risking blackouts or spiking retail electricity prices. Utilities and regulators increasingly require or incentivize large loads to bring net-new supply so households do not subsidize grid expansion and rising capacity costs. Finally, direct long-term contracts lock in predictable pricing—hedging against volatile wholesale power markets—while meeting corporate climate commitments. Financing additional clean or firm capacity such as solar-plus-storage, geothermal, or nuclear provides verifiable "additionality," allowing hyperscalers to scale without cannibalizing existing clean power on fossil-heavy grids.

noweb.answer:
AI hyperscalers contract directly for dedicated new generation primarily because existing US grids lack the spare capacity and transmission infrastructure to connect gigawatt-scale data centers quickly. In most regional markets, utility interconnection queues and high-voltage transmission upgrades take five to ten years—an unacceptable delay in the race to deploy AI compute. Meanwhile, retiring thermal plants and surging electricity demand have tightened grid reserve margins, meaning utilities often cannot supply massive, uninterruptible 24/7 loads off the shelf without risking local reliability. 

Regulators have also stepped in to protect everyday ratepayers, increasingly requiring large data centers to bring their own generation so households do not subsidize costly grid expansions or suffer spiked wholesale power prices. Finally, long-term contracts for dedicated projects—ranging from nuclear and geothermal to natural gas and solar paired with battery storage—lock in predictable power costs hedged against volatile spot markets while securing the verifiable, round-the-clock clean energy hyperscalers need to meet their corporate decarbonization commitments.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Hyperscalers sign contracts for dedicated new generation mainly because the grid doesn't have enough spare capacity for them, and getting new capacity built the normal way is slow. A single AI campus can need hundreds of megawatts to several gigawatts. In regions like PJM, ERCOT and parts of the Southeast, reserve margins are tight and capacity prices have jumped; PJM's auctions set record highs in 2024–25. Utilities often can't promise that much load for years because of transmission upgrades and long interconnection queues. Contracting for specific plants, such as nuclear restarts like Microsoft's Crane deal, Meta's Clinton agreement, gas plants built alongside data centers, or new wind, solar and storage, gets them power sooner.

Cost and climate goals matter too. Long-term power purchase agreements lock in fixed prices instead of volatile wholesale and capacity prices. Paying for new plants also lets companies say their clean energy is "additional," meaning it wouldn't exist without them, which plain grid power doesn't allow. Regulators and utilities are also pushing in this direction. Large-load tariffs and proposals in PJM and Texas increasingly require data centers to bring their own generation or accept curtailment, so other ratepayers don't pay for the extra capacity.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
AI hyperscalers contract directly for dedicated new generation because the US grid often cannot deliver massive, continuous power fast enough to match data center buildouts. Multi-year interconnection queues, transmission bottlenecks, and equipment shortages mean relying on standard utility service can delay gigawatt-scale facilities by years. Funding dedicated or co-located plants secures faster time to power and dependable baseload electricity for energy-intensive AI clusters.

Direct contracts also lock in long-term price certainty, shielding hyperscalers from volatile wholesale power markets and rising capacity costs as regional demand surges. In addition, financing new supply helps meet corporate decarbonization goals through true additionality—backing firm clean sources like nuclear, geothermal, or storage-paired renewables rather than drawing from an existing fossil-heavy grid mix. Finally, bringing their own generation eases regulatory and political scrutiny by demonstrating that hyperscalers are paying for new capacity instead of straining local reliability or shifting grid upgrade costs onto residential ratepayers.

points.why: The response attributes delays to interconnection, transmission, and equipment constraints without establishing that the grid’s surplus generation capacity is largely exhausted.
The response discusses wholesale price risk for hyperscalers and grid upgrade costs for households without linking hyperscalers’ use of existing grid supply to higher retail electricity prices.
The response says funding new generation eases regulatory scrutiny without identifying a growing regulatory requirement that data centers pay for dedicated power.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
AI hyperscalers contract for dedicated new generation because getting hundreds of megawatts at one site can take years. A utility may need new power plants, transmission lines, or substations before it can serve a data center at full capacity. Those timelines can outlast the data center’s construction schedule.

A long-term contract gives a power developer the revenue commitment it needs to finance a new plant. In return, the hyperscaler can lock in some of its power costs and choose a source that meets its needs, whether that’s around-the-clock output or carbon-free electricity. On-site generation can also let a data center open before the grid can supply its full load.

Many of these deals still use the grid to deliver power and balance supply and demand. A contract can get new generation built, but it doesn’t by itself create transmission capacity or guarantee round-the-clock service.

points.why: The response explains delays in serving large loads and treats new generation as one possible upgrade without establishing that spare generation capacity is largely exhausted.
The response discusses the hyperscaler's own power costs without addressing how drawing from existing supply could raise retail customers' bills.
The response explains how contracts finance new plants without identifying any regulatory requirement for data centers to pay for dedicated power.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Buying electricity from the grid works when the local utility can deliver enough power by the date a data center needs it. A large AI campus adds a substantial, nearly continuous load, and new generation or transmission can take years to build. By committing to buy power for many years, a hyperscaler gives a generator the predictable revenue it needs to finance a new plant. In return, the hyperscaler can secure a long-term price for the contracted output and choose generation that helps meet its clean-energy goals.

A direct contract doesn’t necessarily mean a private wire. The plant and data center can both use the grid, and the contract alone neither guarantees uninterrupted service nor moves the campus ahead in the connection queue. Where an on-site plant can serve the campus directly, it can reduce how much power the utility must deliver and may let the campus open sooner.

points.why: The response describes local delivery constraints and long construction timelines without asserting that the existing grid has largely run out of surplus generation capacity.
The response discusses the hyperscaler's contracted price and omits the risk that drawing on existing supply raises retail customers' bills.
The response explains how long-term contracts help finance new plants but identifies no regulatory requirement for data centers to fund their own power.
